episode_title: Don't Run a Country Like a Company

stories.topic: Why stock prices rose during the COVID catastrophe
stories.summary: Ajay warns against reading the stock market index as a report card on the economy or the government. His example is COVID. It was a terrible catastrophe, yet when the US Fed and the RBI cut rates sharply, stock prices went up. Firms were not suddenly better run. Markets were simply discounting future cash flows at a new, lower interest rate.
stories.insight: Stock prices carry real information, but much of what moves an index is the discount rate, not the health of the economy. A country therefore has no clean daily scorecard the way a firm does. Policymakers are partly flying blind.
stories.quote: It was really about a new interest rate for computing NPVs. It was not about the firms were being run much better.

stories.topic: Amit's personal rules (rules vs deals, applied to life)
stories.summary: Taking Ajay's rules-vs-deals frame down to the individual, Amit shares two rules he lives by. First, he avoids negativity: people who complain about others and take a victimhood attitude instead of a can-do one are best avoided, in real life and on Twitter. Second, when he is with someone, he tries to listen and understand their story instead of making himself the centre of it. He admits he doesn't always succeed.
stories.insight: Deciding in advance how you'll handle a whole class of situations saves mental energy and prevents mistakes, just as a state should run on rules rather than case-by-case bargains.
stories.quote: It takes a lot of cognitive energy and leads to mistakes if I do it on a person by person, deal by deal basis.

stories.topic: The Warhol: a quiz question you can work out
stories.summary: Prompted by talk of celebrity culture, Amit reads out a question he set about 15 years ago and later used in a column on quizzing: 'X is a unit of hype. One kilo X is equal to 10.42 days. One mega X is equal to 28.5 years. What is X?' Ajay works it out live. One X is about 0.01 days, roughly 864 seconds. Amit nudges him to round up to fifteen minutes, and Ajay gets it: Andy Warhol, who said everyone will be famous for fifteen minutes. So X is a Warhol. Ajay then counters with his own puzzle, the millihelen.
stories.insight: Amit's philosophy of quizzing: a good question rewards reasoning rather than recall, which makes it fun even for people who aren't trivia buffs.
stories.quote: A good quiz question is one where you can work out the answer.

stories.summary: While discussing the halo effect, Amit recalls a group conversation from earlier that day. Someone kept offering half-baked opinions, and Amit spontaneously laid down a rule: if you state an opinion, you should be able to defend it with an essay-length argument. He admits it sounds extreme, but says there is too much cheap opinion around, much of it received wisdom or tribal allegiance.
stories.insight: A practical filter against the halo effect and Twitter-style hot takes: speak only on what you have actually studied well enough to argue at length.
stories.quote: if you state an opinion here, you should be able to do an essay length argument for it, otherwise don't state it.

stories.summary: News broke that Alice Munro's daughter had said Munro's second husband abused her when she was nine, and that Munro turned a blind eye. Before Amit's flight to DC, Shruti Rajagopalan, a fellow Munro fan, messaged him, disturbed. On the flight he was reading David Brooks's How to Know a Person, which discusses Vivian Gornick's Fierce Attachments: a mother and daughter who understand each other completely and yet not at all. Amit decided to keep loving Munro's work and withhold judgment on her. He still says she clearly did something wrong in minimising her daughter's grief. He separates art from artist, though he adds there are some writers, like Pablo Neruda, he will never read because he knows too much about them.
stories.insight: We usually know only one version of a messy human story. Honest suspension of judgment, without excusing the wrong, is often wiser than a rush to condemn or defend.
stories.quote: Because the world is too complex. We know one story. We don't know the other story. We don't know the other stories.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The whole episode is built on the book's chapter arguing that a country is not a company.
recommendations.reason: Amit says every point in the episode is made there and 'beautifully written'. The video is a companion, 'but please read'.

recommendations.creator: Walt Bogdanich & Michael Forsythe
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode.
recommendations.reason: A cautious recommendation: he finds the book 'a bit mean' and 'one-sided'. It still gives insight into the difficulties of bringing a consulting firm and a consulting approach into complex problems of public policy, which is exactly the episode's theme.

recommendations.creator: David Brooks
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, read on a flight to DC where he recorded a bunch of episodes.
recommendations.reason: It echoes what Amit learned from long-form podcasting: the power of long conversations, of learning to listen, of genuine interest in others, of intentionally building friendships. Brooks himself changed late in life; Oprah remarked on how much he'd changed when he returned to her show years later. Amit also commends Brooks's columns and other books for making us think about our own lives.

recommendations.creator: Vivian Gornick
recommendations.context: Re-recommended because Brooks discusses it in How to Know a Person.
recommendations.reason: Gornick's constant tussle with her mother shows two people who understand each other completely and yet not at all. It is a lesson in the complexity of human relationships and why we shouldn't jump to judgment.

recommendations.creator: Alice Munro
recommendations.context: Amit has spoken before on the show about what her stories mean to him; he revisits her after the news about her daughter.
recommendations.reason: He separates art from artist and says he will continue loving her work while withholding judgment on her as a person.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham

recommendations.reason: Graham's essays are part of where Amit learned that great companies are built by iterating, pivoting and learning by doing. He also names Graham among the finest thinkers to emerge from the business world.

recommendations.creator: John Stossel

recommendations.reason: Stossel's phrase captures why every voluntary interaction is positive-sum, with both sides better off. That is how societies prosper, and it is what coercive states lack.

core_ideas.concept: A country is not a company
core_ideas.explanation: Firms are the source of prosperity, so it feels intuitive that a successful CEO or consultant could run a country. That is a fallacy rooted in top-down instincts that evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes. Running a state differs in its feedback loops, guaranteed survival, coercive power, complexity, rules vs deals, dispersion of power and time horizons.
core_ideas.quote: at the end, gentle reader, we hope to persuade you that the two skills are really completely apart.

core_ideas.concept: Firms are cells, the economy is the organism
core_ideas.explanation: An analogy a friend gave Ajay. The economy is the sum of its firms' productivity, so there is no prosperity without high-productivity firms, just as a body needs healthy cells. But understanding the whole organism is a different body of knowledge from studying one cell at a time.
core_ideas.quote: we should not think that what works at the level of the cell works at the level of the overall organism.

core_ideas.concept: Firms get slapped into shape; governments fly blind
core_ideas.explanation: Firms see daily stock prices, weekly production numbers, monthly profits and market share, so mistakes show up within months and managers can keep debugging. Government has no such loop. The stock index isn't a report card, GDP arrives quarterly with a lag and is badly measured in India, and elections come every five years and turn on base passions. Political feedback also rewards the wrong things: a farm loan waiver wins votes now and can be 'a necessary anesthetic, but it is not the structural change you need.' Constant state and local elections push towards short-termism.
core_ideas.quote: Firms can work well and have a better chance at working well because there are feedback loops and they get slapped into shape.

core_ideas.concept: Social science is a coin in a stormy swimming pool
core_ideas.explanation: Shruti Rajagopalan's analogy, which Amit thinks may come from Don Boudreaux. Testing whether a coin displaces water is easy in a lab beaker. Social science is like dropping the coin into a giant crowded pool in a storm, with forty people swimming and throwing things. Everything is multicausal, so governments can't run clean A/B tests the way a business choosing between polyester blends can.
core_ideas.quote: You are in a crowded hundred meter by hundred meter swimming pool. There is a storm overhead, there are forty people swimming inside and throwing things, and you're trying to drop a coin there.

core_ideas.explanation: The threat of bankruptcy disciplines every firm. A CBI, RBI, SEBI or ministry is guaranteed to exist however badly it performs. For many state bodies the right metaphor for monopoly power is not supernormal profits but unquestioned access to coercive power. Losing the fear of death breeds complacence and misbehaviour.
core_ideas.quote: If you are the defense ministry of India, you are the defense ministry of India. I mean you could lose wars, many things could go wrong, but basically your life is assured.

core_ideas.concept: Monopoly and failure are state problems, not market problems
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that monopolies don't arise under genuine free-market competition. They come either from state interference that shields a crony, or from the state itself: violence, money, and the many monopolies it sets up. Likewise, market failure is rare while government failure is ubiquitous, because of the state's incentives and structure. Meanwhile, competing private firms deliver Schumpeter's creative destruction.
core_ideas.quote: So I would say that if you're thinking monopoly, it's a problem with the state.

core_ideas.concept: Coercion is core to the state
core_ideas.explanation: A firm is a bundle of voluntary contracts with customers, employees and other firms; firms that hire goons are a scummy minority who belong in jail. Following Max Weber's definition of the state as a monopoly of physical violence in a territory, the state is inherently coercive. So lessons from running firms don't carry over, and as Lord Acton warned, the same person will face very different incentives at the head of government.
core_ideas.quote: That to be the state is to have coercive power.

core_ideas.concept: Voluntary exchange: the double thank you and the market as conversation
core_ideas.explanation: Every voluntary exchange leaves both sides better off, which is how economies grow. Amit also pictures the market as a vast conversation: firms pitch to customers, rivals offer to serve them better, and teams inside firms tweak designs, all of which helps people serve others and understand themselves better. The state has no need to hold that conversation; it can simply take.
core_ideas.quote: every voluntary interaction between two people creates what John Stossel calls a double thank you moment. Both people are better off.

core_ideas.explanation: Even a large firm is simple next to a government spread across countless departments and offices, often with conflicting objectives, all interacting with society. Ajay, who has worked in both worlds, says you must scale back your ambition of even measuring and understanding government, let alone changing it.
core_ideas.quote: in firms I sort of feel that this is nice, this is clean, this is solvable, we can do this. Whereas with government, it is like, my God, this is too hard. This is impossibly complicated.

core_ideas.concept: Don't trade the real target for easy wins
core_ideas.explanation: Because big problems are complex and progress can't be attributed quickly, many in development and policy retreat to small problems they can solve with an RCT and claim credit for. These don't move the needle on poverty. Amit's advice to young people in the ideas and policy world: resist easy wins pursued for career advancement or self-gratification.
core_ideas.quote: don't take your eye off the target. The target is real long term change.

core_ideas.concept: Bias for action: an open disagreement
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay is uneasy with the startup slogan even for firms: thinking is precious, and shooting first is superficial. In government it is 'truly dangerous'. You must identify the market failure, find the lowest-cost intervention, reshape incentives and negotiate the political economy. Amit agrees about the state but insists firms need a bias for action, since great companies iterate and pivot, and thinkers like Jeff Bezos combined action with deep thought. They agree it's not a binary; the real enemy is reflexive short-termism.
core_ideas.quote: Thinking is precious, is always precious.

core_ideas.explanation: A small firm can live deal to deal as a hustler. A large one like McDonald's must move to standard contracts with franchisees, or it collapses into complexity and corruption. The state, the most complex organisation of all, must run on rules. That gives policy coherence across its many arms and over time, and it lets private actors plan for the long term. Article 14 also requires equal treatment. The state's job is to set stable rules that reshape incentives, not to make steel or cut individual bargains.
core_ideas.quote: The engagement between a government and a private person can absolutely not be deals. That would not be rule of law, it would be rule of men.

core_ideas.explanation: A friend's image: a tiny firm is cooking, with one cook choosing every ingredient. A growing firm is gardening: you create conditions, culture, incentives and checks, and run a portfolio of bets. In a country as diverse as India, a firm should be an octopus with many thinking nodes, not a starfish with one brain. For the state there is no option. Power is deliberately split into legislature, executive and judiciary, and into union, state, city and village governments under the subsidiarity principle.
core_ideas.quote: there's a single big insight in two thousand years of politics and political philosophy, it is this one sentence, dispersion of power.

core_ideas.explanation: An autocratic firm costs society little, since fifty rivals will serve customers and the firm learns or dies. But we wrongly credit a superstar CEO like Jack Welch for what a large, dispersed organisation achieved. We do the same with heads of government, praising or opposing a leader for outcomes that came from the wider policy ecosystem.
core_ideas.quote: something right may have emerged out of a policy ecosystem within the state, which that individual didn't really affect.

core_ideas.concept: Time horizons and the inexorable policy pipeline
core_ideas.explanation: High cost of capital in India's weak financial system makes firms short-sighted: in a net present value calculation with a high rate, the future barely counts, and owners expect to sell within three years. Government must play a hundred-year game to close the 9x per-capita GDP gap with America. Reform moves through a pipeline: data, research, theories of change, public debate, expert committees, drafting laws, then building state capacity. It takes 10 to 20 years, a rhythm most private-sector people aren't used to.
core_ideas.quote: there is a policy pipeline and it is inexorable. It is a damn pipeline. There is no way to reach the end without every step of the way.

core_ideas.concept: Live by the longest and shortest time horizons
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's personal application. Think about your life as a whole rather than chasing one immediate gratification after another, but recognise that life is a succession of days. He used to fixate on awards to win and books to write. Grand goals are toxic, because achieving them only reveals grander ones. Echoing Annie Dillard, a day is your life: build the best possible day and a great life follows.
core_ideas.quote: But if you just build your days, like a day is not a waiting room in which you sit and you wait for your life to happen.

core_ideas.concept: Politics, governance and policy are different games
core_ideas.explanation: Running a firm well doesn't disqualify someone from governing. Flexible thinkers like Paul Graham, Naval Ravikant or Jeff Bezos could retool, but must change how they think. Equally, politicians who have mastered the game of retail politics often arrive in government with no feel for governance (substance over narrative, working with people, understanding institutions) or for the economy. Citizens should hold everyone to high standards.
core_ideas.quote: the people who come to power very often are people who have mastered one game, and that is a game of politics. And the game of governance is very different.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay admires India's post-1990s business, consulting and finance talent as world-class, yet warns against assuming it transfers to public policy. Amit names the bias: excellence in one field creates a halo, so people assume you're expert elsewhere, like a microbiologist dispensing wisdom on all of medicine. His antidote is to opine only on what you've studied.
core_ideas.quote: if you excel in one area, it's almost like there's a halo around you, and people assume that this person will excel in other areas.

core_ideas.explanation: At a restaurant, everyone orders what they like from the menu. In a democracy, if three vote for seafood, the fourth eats it or goes hungry, even if allergic to prawns. The 'political marketplace' metaphor breaks down because democracy risks majoritarianism. Hence the need for a republic, with a constitution protecting individuals and minorities from the state.
core_ideas.quote: it's not enough to be a democracy. You need to be a republic where you have a constitution protecting the people from the state, not the other way around.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit opens by contrasting the dark triad ('the three characteristics that make up serial killers') with a 'light triad' of three Fs: 'firms, finance, and freedom'. He then nominates a bad F: 'Fallacy should be part of the dark triad of bad economic thinking. We'll figure out the other two Fs later.'

Ajay on a government-created monopoly that blocks private and foreign competitors: 'this is the new Air India. It will sit here, it will lord over the society and people will clap saying, Oh, it is so great India now has planes.' Amit notes that it sounds dystopian, except it's real.

Ajay, deflating the 'China model' buzz: 'There is nothing a Fortune 500 company CEO wants to do more than to fly into a third world country, shake hands with a strong man, and make a deal.' People call this decisive government; he says it should embarrass us.
Ajay's dry aside on India's layers of government: 'a union government and a little confused creature called a state government and a city government or a village government.'
After the hosts can't settle the bias-for-action debate, Amit invites viewers to ask for a full episode on it: 'Though Ajay might say, Let us not do it. That will be bias for action.'
Amit's jab at development economists who pick easy problems: they run an RCT, declare 'I have solved it', and say 'give me credit for it, give me a Nobel prize', while poverty doesn't budge.

The celebrity exchange. Ajay: 'In the modern celebrity culture, a company is like a country.' Amit: 'Are you a celebrity? Of course not. You're not a celebrity. Readers kindly comment and let us know if that is true.' Ajay: 'A celebrity is one who is famous for being famous. A celebrity is one whose name is worth more than her services.'
Ajay's counter-puzzle to Amit's Warhol quiz: 'What is a millihelen?' Helen's was 'the beauty that launched a thousand ships. So millihelen is the beauty that will launch one ship.' Amit: 'Nice one.'
Amit says a flexible-minded business leader could learn to govern, 'But your standard issue McKinsey consultant will just fuck it up.'
Amit on his rule of listening rather than making himself the centre: 'one is male and hardwired like a male, we are the center of the universe, but one can make an effort.'
Andy Warhol's line that everyone in the world will be famous for fifteen minutes: the basis of Amit's 'unit of hype', the Warhol, in which a kilo-Warhol is 10.42 days.
Max Weber's definition of the state as a community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of physical violence in a given territory, cited by Ajay to show coercion is the essence of the state.
Lord Acton's 'power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely', which Amit uses to explain why the same person behaves differently at the head of a firm and of a government.
Schumpeter's 'creative destruction', which Amit invokes for the hundreds of firms competing in a field: most fail, and that is good for society, whereas there is only one government.
Ronald Coase on the firm and Hayek on prices, recalled from the show's 'Four Papers' episode as foundations for thinking about firms versus the complexity of society.
Article 14 of the Indian Constitution (equal treatment). McDonald's can legally strike different deals with different franchisees; the state cannot treat citizens differently.
Six Sigma and Google's self-invocation to 'do no evil', which Amit cites as examples of firms adopting rules once they reach scale.
Jack Welch at GE, Amit's example of how we turn CEOs into superstar figures and credit one person for what a dispersed organisation achieved.
Annie Dillard: 'How you spend your days is, of course, how you spend your life', Amit's corrective to chasing grand goals.
Pablo Neruda: Amit separates art from artist, but names Neruda as someone he will never read 'because I know too much about them.'
